clinician.trajectory_summary: An 86-year-old woman with a history of diabetes, hypertension, angina pectoris, and chronic kidney disease presented with sudden-onset abdominal pain. Initial laboratory tests revealed severe metabolic lactic acidosis (pH 7.110, lactate 9.1 mmol/L), leukocytosis, marked inflammatory signs, renal dysfunction, and a significantly elevated serum phosphate level (14.4 mg/dL). An initial abdominal contrast-enhanced CT scan showed dilated colon and small intestine with fluids but ruled out complete/closed-loop obstruction, free air, ascites, and specific signs of occlusive ischemic bowel (no absence of bowel wall enhancement, pneumatosis intestinalis, hepatic portal venous gas, or bowel wall thickening). At admission, she exhibited signs of hypoperfusion (cold limbs, mottled skin) and her systolic blood pressure rapidly decreased from 139 mmHg to 60 mmHg within one hour, leading to shock. Due to clinical deterioration, an emergency laparotomy was performed six hours after admission. Surgical findings revealed discontinuously necrotic ileum and whole colon (except for the sigmoid), despite pulsation of the superior mesenteric artery, and no bowel obstruction. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with NOMI, and underwent ileal resection, subtotal colectomy, and jejunostomy.
